title: State of U.P. v. C.O.D. Chheoki Employees' Cooperative Society Ltd.
bench: Justice K. Ramaswamy, Justice D.P. Wadhwa
facts_summary: The constitutional validity of statutory amendments regulating management committees of co-operative societies was challenged by member societies claiming fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(c). The state government enacted provisions to ensure representative governance and public interest oversight.
ratio_decidendi: Members of a co-operative society have no fundamental right to management independent of statutory regulation. The right to form an association under Article 19(1)(c) does not include a fundamental right to manage a statutory co-operative society contrary to statutory provisions.
holding: Upheld state regulation over co-operative societies management committees. Statutory rules governing appointment of administrators under Section 27A principles are constitutional and bind all member societies.

title: Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India
facts_summary: In a contempt proceeding, the Supreme Court suspended a senior advocate from practicing law by invoking plenary powers under Article 142. The Supreme Court Bar Association challenged whether Article 142 permits overriding statutory provisions of the Advocates Act regarding professional misconduct.
ratio_decidendi: Powers under Article 142 are supplementary and cannot supplant substantive statutory provisions governing professional misconduct regulated by the Bar Council under the Advocates Act. Contempt jurisdiction cannot be used to permanently punish an advocate by revoking their license to practice.
holding: The Court clarified limits of Article 142; disciplinary action against advocates rests primarily with Bar Councils under statutory procedure.

title: T.P. Senkumar, IPS v. Union of India and Others
bench: Justice Madan B. Lokur, Justice Deepak Gupta
facts_summary: The State Government arbitrarily removed the Director General of Police (DGP) prior to the completion of his statutory tenure of two years, alleging public dissatisfaction following two specific criminal incidents.
ratio_decidendi: High constitutional and administrative functionaries cannot be removed arbitrarily or on subjective dissatisfaction without cogent material and adherence to statutory tenure protections. Arbitrary state action violates Article 14.
holding: Directed reinstatement of the Kerala State Police Chief and held that the executive could not short-circuit the petitioner's protected tenure through arbitrary transfer/removal.

title: Board of Control for Cricket in India v. Cricket Association of Bihar
bench: Justice T.S. Thakur, Justice F.M. Ibrahim Kalifulla
facts_summary: A writ petition under Article 226 was filed against BCCI regarding conflict of interest of office bearers participating in IPL commercial interests and failure to maintain transparency in cricket administration.
ratio_decidendi: Even if an organization is a private body registered under Societies Registration Act, if it performs public functions affecting public domain, it is amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution.
holding: BCCI held subject to Article 226 writ jurisdiction due to public functions; Mudgal and Lodha Committees appointed to reform governance.

title: Rajya Vokkaligara Sangha v. State of Karnataka
facts_summary: Members and office bearers of Rajya Vokkaligara Sangha challenged the State Government's decision to appoint an Administrator under Section 27A, alleging that the elected management had been displaced without satisfying statutory preconditions and fair procedure.
ratio_decidendi: Supersession of an elected society body under Section 27A has serious civil consequences. The State must therefore act on objective material, remain within the four corners of the statute, and comply with natural justice; arbitrary or extraneous intervention is open to correction under Article 226.
holding: Treated the State's appointment of an Administrator to the Sangha as reviewable under Article 226 and measured the action against Section 27A's statutory preconditions and natural justice requirements.

title: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
bench: Justice S. Ratnavel Pandian, Justice K. Jayachandra Reddy
facts_summary: Political opponent filed an FIR alleging corruption and assets disproportionate to known sources of income against a former Chief Minister. High Court quashed the FIR using inherent powers.
ratio_decidendi: Laid down seven broad categories of cases where inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC or Article 226 can be exercised to quash criminal proceedings, including where allegations in FIR do not disclose a cognizable offense or where prosecution is maliciously instituted.
holding: Set aside High Court order quashing FIR, but established landmark guidelines for quashing criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC.

title: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
facts_summary: Father of a kidnapped minor girl approached police to register FIR. Police delayed registration demanding bribes and conducting informal inquiry. Writ petition filed seeking mandatory FIR registration.
ratio_decidendi: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offense. No preliminary inquiry is permissible in such cases except in specific narrow exceptions like matrimonial or commercial disputes with time-bound limits.
holding: Issued mandatory directives to police officers across India for immediate FIR registration upon receipt of cognizable offense details.

title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
bench: Justice Chandramauli Kr. Prasad, Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose
facts_summary: Husband apprehended arrest in a case registered under Section 498A IPC and Dowry Prohibition Act. Police routinely arrested accused persons without satisfaction of necessity under Section 41 CrPC.
ratio_decidendi: Arrest should not be automatic or mechanical in offenses punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Police officers must satisfy conditions under Section 41 CrPC and issue notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC prior to making arrest.
holding: Mandated check-lists for police and magistrates under Section 41/41A CrPC to prevent unnecessary arrests in matrimonial and minor offenses.

title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation
bench: Justice S. Abdul Nazeer, Justice J.K. Maheshwari
facts_summary: CBI and trial courts were routinely issuing non-bailable warrants and remanding accused persons to custody upon filing of chargesheet even when accused was not arrested during investigation.
ratio_decidendi: Bail is the rule and jail is an exception. Filing of chargesheet does not necessitate remand to judicial custody if the accused cooperated during investigation and complied with Section 41A notice.
holding: Categorized offenses into four groups (A, B, C, D) and issued comprehensive bail guidelines restricting unnecessary custodial detention.

title: Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
bench: Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, Justice M.R. Shah, Justice Sanjiv Khanna
facts_summary: High Courts were routinely passing blanket interim orders staying investigation or ordering 'no coercive steps' while entertaining petitions under Section 482 CrPC.
ratio_decidendi: Police have a statutory right to investigate cognizable offenses. High Courts should not routinely stay investigation or pass 'no coercive steps' interim orders unless extraordinary case of abuse of process is demonstrated.
holding: Discouraged interim stay orders on criminal investigations under Section 482 CrPC except in rarest of rare cases.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
facts_summary: Constitutional challenge to the Aadhaar biometric identification scheme raised the core legal question of whether privacy is a fundamental right protected under the Constitution of India.
ratio_decidendi: Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21 and part of freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. State intrusion must satisfy legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality tests.
holding: Unanimously held Right to Privacy as a fundamental right; overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held otherwise.

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
facts_summary: Passport of the petitioner was impounded by the Regional Passport Officer under statutory provisions without disclosing reasons or offering an opportunity of hearing.
ratio_decidendi: 'Procedure established by law' under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; it must satisfy the test of reasonableness, fairness, and natural justice under Article 14. Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an interconnected golden triangle.
holding: Impounding order declared invalid for violating audi alteram partem; radically expanded the scope of personal liberty under Article 21.

title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
facts_summary: Writ petitions filed by LGBTQ+ individuals challenging the penalization of consensual sexual acts in private under Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code.
ratio_decidendi: Section 377 IPC, in so far as it penalizes consensual sexual acts between adults in private, violates Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21. Constitutional morality prevails over majoritarian morality.
holding: Struck down Section 377 IPC to the extent of consensual adult acts in private; upheld individual autonomy, dignity, and equality.

title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
bench: Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman
facts_summary: Two young women were arrested under Section 66A of the Information Technology Act for posting comments on social media questioning a city shutdown. Public interest litigations challenged Section 66A as unconstitutionally vague.
ratio_decidendi: Section 66A of the IT Act casts a wide net penalizing speech that is offensive or annoying without defining precise boundaries, exceeding reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). A law creating a criminal offense must be clear and precise.
holding: Section 66A IT Act struck down in its entirety as unconstitutional for violating freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
facts_summary: Religious math leader challenged Kerala land reform acts under Article 26. The 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments were challenged, raising the scope of Parliament's amending power under Article 368.
ratio_decidendi: While Parliament has broad power to amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368, it cannot alter, destroy, or abrogate the 'Basic Structure' or essential framework of the Constitution.
holding: Formulated the Basic Structure Doctrine, limiting parliamentary amending power to preserve fundamental constitutional features.
